[48;5;237m❯ [38;5;231mNo tools. Begin your reply with the word ZQX, then write about 300 words on the history of lighthouses as plain paragraphs.[39m                                                                           

[38;5;231m[49m●[39m ZQX. People have marked dangerous coasts with fire for more than two thousand years. The most famous early lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria, built in Egypt around 280 BC under Ptolemy II. It
  stood well over 100 meters tall and burned a fire at its top that ships could reportedly see from far out at sea. It survived for centuries before earthquakes brought it down in the 1300s. Its name
  lives on in several languages: "faro" in Spanish and Italian and "phare" in French both mean lighthouse.

  The Romans built lighthouses across their empire, from Dover in England to the Tower of Hercules in northern Spain, which is still in use today. After Rome fell, upkeep stopped and many towers
  crumbled. Through the Middle Ages, coastal lights were mostly kept by monasteries, towns, or merchant guilds. They usually burned wood, coal, or candles, which gave a weak, smoky light.

  Big changes came in the 1700s and 1800s as sea trade grew. Builders learned to put towers on open rocks, where storms had wrecked earlier attempts. John Smeaton's Eddystone Lighthouse, finished in
  1759, used interlocking granite blocks and set the pattern for later stone towers. Oil lamps with reflectors replaced open fires and gave a brighter, steadier light.

  The biggest jump came in 1822, when the French engineer Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens. It used rings of glass prisms to bend scattered light into one strong beam. A Fresnel lens could
  be seen more than 20 miles away, and it soon spread around the world.

  In the 1900s, electric lamps replaced oil, and lights were automated so keepers were no longer needed. Today, satellite navigation does most of the work lighthouses once did. Many towers still
  shine, but they are now kept mainly as historic landmarks and backup aids for ships.

[48;5;237m❯ [38;5;231mNo tools. Write about 250 words on how tides work: a short heading, two paragraphs, a bulleted list of three items with some [1mbold[0m[38;5;231m[48;5;237m and [38;5;153minline code[38;5;231m, then a final paragraph.[39m                            

[38;5;231m[49m●[39m [1mHow Tides Work

[0m  Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, and the Moon's gravity drives most of it. Gravity gets weaker with distance. Because of that, the Moon pulls hardest on the side of Earth facing it,
  less on Earth's center, and least on the far side. The water facing the Moon bulges toward it. On the far side, the Moon pulls the solid Earth away from the water more than it pulls the water
  itself, so a second bulge forms there.
